name: Hall probe
description: A strip of metal carrying a current, in your solenoid's field (B along the strip's length, out of the board when positive; the yellow coil, top right). The field pushes the moving electrons sideways (the Lorentz force) until the charge they pile on one side holds the rest back: a voltage across the strip, the Hall voltage, $V_H \approx I B/(n q)$ (per unit length). The two contacts on the strip's sides read it, floating: no current flows through them. Try the field's whole range: weak, the electrons' paths barely bend; strong, they curl into small circles between collisions. Make a current between 2.7 and 3.5 flow into the right end and the top contact sit between 3.5 and 6 below the bottom one (averaged over $t = 10$ to $80$). Which way must the field point? Electrons are negative.

reality.represents: A Hall probe: the voltage across a current in a magnetic field

remarks.detail: The field pushes the moving carriers sideways until the charge they pile up holds the rest back; at strong fields the voltage grows ever more slowly (the Hall factor falls towards 1, and the end contacts short it).

remarks.line: A semiconductor, as real probes are
remarks.detail: By its ratios the strip is n-type germanium (the Scales section); real Hall probes are semiconductors for the reason Few carriers or many shows.
The floating side contacts read the potential as an ideal voltmeter does, through a capacitance of 1 to ground, drawing no current.

The strip is infinitely long along z, its carriers lines of charge moving as one: currents are per unit length, and the noise is larger than a real conductor's, whose carriers move independently along its length.
